The reproductive biology of the Lesser African threadfin (Galeoides decadactylus) has been studied primarily in the coastal waters of the eastern Atlantic, where individuals attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of 11.6 cm [Lp = 11.6 cm]. Field studies indicate that the gonadosomatic index (GSI) peaked at 9.6% [GSI = 9.6%] during the reproductive season at a water temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. This figure was recorded at a water temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], which is typical for the tropical inshore habitats this threadfin occupies. Breeding activity appears to be protracted, with gravid females observed over several months of the year.

Neonates of Galeoides decadactylus emerge from pelagic eggs that are approximately 0.775 millimeters in diameter, and the calculated wet weight at birth is extremely low at 0.00024 grams [Wwb = 0.00024 grams]. This minute birth mass, characteristic of species with pelagic, planktotrophic larvae, reflects the energetic constraint imposed by producing large numbers of small offspring. The newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are lecithotrophic and depend entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-eclosion before transitioning to first exogenous feeding. The larval period is brief relative to many tropical marine teleosts, and the rapid uptake of planktonic prey allows for substantial growth during the pelagic phase. The minute initial size of the prolarvae, however, renders them highly vulnerable to starvation and predation, and only a small fraction of the initial cohort is expected to survive through the larval-juvenile transition. This high early mortality is a common trait among broadcast spawners.

As the juvenile fish grow and recruit to benthic habitats, their growth trajectory becomes gradually asymptotic. The ultimate total length recorded for Galeoides decadactylus in sampled populations reaches approximately 50 centimeters [Li = approximately 50 centimeters], a size that is consistent among large adults from the Gulf of Guinea. Corresponding to this asymptotic length, the ultimate body mass attained by fully grown individuals is approximately 1467 grams [Wwi = approximately 1467 grams], a value that was derived from length–weight regressions fitted to a substantial sample of market-caught specimens. This body mass represents a considerable gain from the sub-milligram neonate and highlights the capacity for extensive somatic growth across the life cycle. The relationship between length and weight in this species is strongly allometric, reflecting a relatively deep-bodied and robust adult morphology. Older individuals often dominate the largest size classes, and it is these large breeders that contribute the bulk of reproductive output to the next generation.

Longevity in Galeoides decadactylus under natural conditions has been estimated from length-frequency analysis and otolith readings. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 16 years when expressed in days, which amounts to approximately 5840 days [am = approximately 5840 days], a relatively extended life span for a tropical coastal fis at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]h of this size. This longevity estimate is based on individuals maintained at a water temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], which is representative of the thermal regime in its core habitat. The capacity to live for well over a decade allows for repeated reproductive investment across multiple breeding seasons, consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy. Such a long reproductive lifespan offsets the extremely high mortality experienced during the pelagic larval and early juvenile stages, providing multiple opportunities for successful recruitment over an individual’s lifetime. This pattern is common among tropical sciaenids and other demersal spawners.

Comparisons with congeneric species within the family Polynemidae reveal that the life history of Galeoides decadactylus is characterized by a conservative pace, with a relatively large ultimate size and a prolonged reproductive window. The gonadosomatic index remained near 9.6% [GSI = 9.6%] during peak reproductive activity at 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. The combination of a large ultimate weight of 1467 grams [Wwi = 1467 grams] and a long lifespan exceeding 5800 days (5840 days) [am = 5840 days] places this species toward the slower end of the life-history continuum among Polynemidae at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. This strategy likely confers a demographic advantage in environments where larval survival is unpredictable and variable. The species is also subject to moderate fishing pressure across its range, and such a life-history profile may render it vulnerable to overexploitation if large, fecund individuals are selectively removed from the population. Ongoing conservation assessments are needed to ensure sustainable harvest levels.
